en: Thus have I heard— Majjhima Nikāya 80, the Vekhanasasutta.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Then the wanderer Vekhanassa approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him.
When they had concluded their courteous and amiable conversation, he stood to one side.
Standing to one side, the wanderer Vekhanassa uttered this inspired utterance in the presence of the Blessed One:
“This is the supreme beauty! This is the supreme beauty!
“But why, Kaccāna, do you speak thus?”
“‘This is the supreme beauty, this is the supreme beauty’—
what, Kaccāna, is that supreme beauty?
“That beauty, Master Gotama, beyond which there is no other beauty higher or more sublime— that is the supreme beauty.”
“But what, Kaccāna, is that beauty beyond which there is no other beauty higher or more sublime?
“That beauty, Master Gotama, beyond which there is no other beauty higher or more sublime—that is the supreme beauty.
“Kaccāna, you might well speak at length regarding this:”
“Master Gotama, you say: ‘That complexion beyond which no other complexion is higher or more sublime—that is the supreme complexion,’ yet you do not point out what that complexion is.
It is just as if, Kaccāna, a man were to say:
‘I desire and long for the most beautiful woman in this country.’”
They would say to him:

"Good man, as for that most beautiful woman in the land whom you desire and lust after, do you know whether that most beautiful woman in the land is a khattiya woman, a brahmin woman, a vessa woman, or a sudda woman?
Being asked thus, he would say: "No."
They would say to him:
"O man, as for that 'Beauty of the Land' whom you desire and love, do you know that Beauty of the Land by name or by clan...
[and so on] ...whether she is tall or short or of medium height, or whether she is dark, or fair, or of ruddy complexion?"
‘Does it blow in such-and-such a village, town, or city?
Being asked thus, he would say, ‘No.
Then they would say to him:
"O man, do you desire and long for that which you neither know nor see?
Being asked thus, he would say, "Yes.
What do you think, Kaccāna?
“But if this is so, does it not follow that the speech of that man turns out to be unconvincing?
“Certainly, Master Gotama, if this is so, the speech of that man turns out to be unconvincing.

“In the same way, Kaccāna, you say: ‘Master Gotama, there is no other complexion superior or more excellent than this; that is the supreme complexion,’ yet you do not specify what that complexion is.”

“Just as, Master Gotama, a beautiful beryl gem of pure birth, cut with eight facets and well-polished, placed on a white cloth, shines, glows, and radiates—of such a color is the self, healthy after death.
“What do you think, Kaccāna?
Regarding that beautiful beryl gem of pure birth, cut with eight facets and well-polished, placed on a white cloth...”
"It shines, it glows, and it radiates; or else, in the thick darkness of the night, there is the glow-worm—of these two colors, which one is more excellent and more sublime?
"The glow-worm, Master Gotama, in the thick darkness of the night, is the more excellent and more sublime of these two colors."
“What do you think, Kaccāna?
Between a glowworm in the thick darkness of the night and an oil lamp in the thick darkness of the night, which of these two appearances is more excellent and more sublime?
“The one that is the oil lamp in the thick darkness of the night, Master Gotama; this is more excellent and more sublime than the other two appearances.”
“What do you think, Kaccāna:
between a lamp of oil in the thick darkness of the night and a great mass of fire in the thick darkness of the night, which of these two appearances is more excellent and more sublime?
“Sir Gotama, that great mass of fire in the thick darkness of the night is more excellent and more sublime than these two appearances.”
“What do you think, Kaccāna?
Between a great mass of fire in the pitch-black darkness of night and the morning star at dawn on a clear,
cloudless night— which of these two colors is more excellent?”
“...and which is more excellent?
“That star Osadhi, Master Gotama, when it appears at the break of dawn on a clear night when the clouds have vanished—this is more radiant and more excellent than both of those colors.
“What do you think, Kaccāna?”
“Between the color of the morning star when the night has passed and the sky is clear and cloudless,
and the color of the moon at midnight on the fifteenth day of the lunar month, when the full-moon uposatha is observed and the sky is clear and cloudless—
of these two colors, which is more excellent and more sublime?”

“Master Gotama, on the fifteenth day of the uposatha, when the sky is clear and free of clouds, this moon that shines at the time of midnight—this is more excellent and more sublime than those two colors.
“What do you think, Kaccāna?
Is it the case that on the fifteenth day of the uposatha, when the sky is clear and free of clouds, [the moon] shines at the time of midnight...”
“The moon, or the sun when it shines at midday in the last month of the rainy season during the autumn time,
when the sky is clear and free of clouds— of these two colors, which color is more excellent and more sublime? “That which is the sun, Master Gotama,
in the last month of the rainy season during the autumn time, when the sky is clear and free of clouds...”
“At midday, when the sun is at its zenith—this radiance is more excellent and more sublime than both of these.
“Indeed, Kaccāna, there are many, many more devas who do not even equal the radiance of these two, the moon and the sun; I know them.
And yet, I do not say:”
"There is no other beauty higher or more sublime than this.
Yet you, Kaccāna, say: "That beauty which is inferior and more loathsome than that of the glowworm is the supreme beauty," and you do not define what that beauty is.
There are, Kaccāna, these five strands of sensual pleasure.
Which five?
Forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, pleasing, endearing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust;
sounds cognizable by the ear … [and so on] … [as above].
Odors cognizable by the nose...
tastes cognizable by the tongue...
tangibles cognizable by the body that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual pleasure, and provocative of lust—
“Kaccāna, these are the five cords of sensual pleasure.
Kaccāna, whatever happiness and joy arise dependent upon these five cords of sensual pleasure, this is called sensual pleasure.
Thus, among sensual pleasures there is the pleasure of sensual desire; compared to the pleasure of sensual desire, the pleasure of the peak of sensual desire is declared to be supreme therein.”
When this was said, the wanderer Vekhanassa said this to the Blessed One:
“It is wonderful, Master Gotama! It is marvelous, Master Gotama!
How well this has been spoken by Master Gotama!”
“‘In sensual pleasures there is sensual happiness; in sensual happiness, the supreme happiness of sensuality is declared to be the highest therein.
‘In sensual pleasures, Master Gotama, there is sensual happiness; in sensual happiness, the supreme happiness of sensuality is declared to be the highest therein.
“This, Kaccāna, is difficult for you to understand, since you hold a different view, have different inclinations, different tastes, follow a different discipline, and have a different teacher.”
“Either sensual pleasures, or the pleasure of sensual desires, or the supreme pleasure of sensual desires.

“Kaccāna, those bhikkhus who are arahants, whose taints are destroyed, who have lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained their own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and are completely liberated through final knowledge—they would indeed know this:
whether it be sensual pleasures, the pleasure of sensual desires, or the supreme pleasure of sensual desires.”
When this was said, the wanderer Vekhanassa became angry and displeased; reviling the Blessed One, disparaging the Blessed One, and speaking against the Blessed One, he said to the Blessed One:
"The ascetic Gotama will be proven wrong. And he said this to the Blessed One:
"In this very way, there are some ascetics and brahmins here who, not knowing the past and not seeing the future, nevertheless..."
‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being’—thus they claim to understand.
Yet their assertion turns out to be merely laughable, merely nominal, merely empty, and merely hollow.
“Kaccāna, those ascetics and brahmins who, not knowing the past and not seeing the future, [claim such things]...”
‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being’—thus they claim to understand.
This is the legitimate refutation of them according to the Dhamma.
Furthermore, Kaccāna, let alone the past, let alone the future.
"Let a wise man, free from deceit and guile, upright by nature, come; I shall instruct him, I shall teach him the Dhamma.
Practicing according to the instruction, before long he will himself know and himself see:
'Thus, indeed, there is a complete release from bondage—that is, from the bondage of ignorance.'"
"Just as, Kaccāna, a young boy, tender and lying on his back, might be bound with bonds consisting of five strands—
bonds of thread— and as those bonds were released through his growth and the maturation of his faculties,
he would know, 'I am free,' yet not [perceive] the bond."
“In the same way, Kaccāna, when a wise person who is not fraudulent, not deceitful, and upright by nature comes to me, saying, ‘I instruct;
I teach the Dhamma,’ and practices according to that instruction, before long he will know for himself and see for himself:
‘Thus indeed is there right liberation from bondage, namely, from the bondage of ignorance.’”
When this was said, the wanderer Vekhanasa said this to the Blessed One:
“Magnificent, Master Gotama!
… [as before] … May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life shall last.”
The Vekhanasa Sutta, the tenth, is finished.
The third chapter, the Chapter on Wanderers, is finished.
Its summary verse:
Puṇḍarīka, Aggisahaka, and Kathina by name;
Dīghanakha, who was of the Bhāradvāja clan;
Sandaka, Udāyin, and Muṇḍikaputta.
Maṇika, Tathākaccāna, and Varavagga.
